newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says breakthrough reached on new CFE treaty.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says breakthrough reached on new CFE treaty.

text.p: A group of 30 nations that includes all NATO members and their former Warsaw Pact enemies reached a framework accord on Wednesday to further reduce the conventional arms stationed in Europe, the White House said.

The 30 countries are parties to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe Treaty (CFE), which limits the number of tanks, artillery pieces, aircraft and other non-nuclear arms the states can hold in Europe and where they can be placed.

The White House said the agreement in principle reached in Vienna on Wednesday would adapt that treaty for the post-Cold War era, changing the structure of these limits and reducing the overall amount of such equipment in the relevant area.

"In effect, we've taken a treaty that was the product of the Cold War, negotiated with the Soviet Union, and taken a huge step today in adapting it to the new Europe," White House arms control expert Bob Bell told reporters.

"The 30 states collectively have agreed that ... there will be significantly less equipment permitted in the area of application in Europe, which goes from the Atlantic to the Urals, than there was under the original treaty," he added.

Bell said the outline accord would replace the old CFE treaty, which allowed one overall amount of equipment for the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation members and an equal amount for the Warsaw Pact, with a system setting national ceilings.
The new treaty, expected to be concluded within a year, would fix ceilings on the amount of equipment that a given country could station on its soil.
The White House official said the exact ceilings had not been decided, adding there was a lot of negotiation yet to come before a final agreement would be concluded.

He said the new treaty would also adopt the substance of the so-called "flank agreement" ratified this year that loosened constraints on Russia's deployment of conventional forces to meet security threats in the north Caucasus.

Russia had argued that the overall ceilings set in 1990 needed to be revised because of political changes on the continent since then, including the collapse of the Soviet Union and the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact.
